title: Stop Adding & Start Improving
author: Caiti Wade
summary: Caiti Wade challenges a common assumption in school professional-development culture: that once teachers 'already do' a technique like checking for understanding, there is no further value in revisiting it. Drawing on her own six years of repeatedly returning to checking-for-understanding training -- as both learner and presenter, even at researchED conferences -- she argues that expertise increases rather than removes the responsibility to keep refining practice, and that professional learning is iterative, not seasonal. Wade attributes much of the problem to schools treating PD like a menu, sampling new frameworks briefly before moving to the next trend, when implementation research shows moving from initial adoption to genuine fidelity takes years; abandoning an initiative after a single term produces only 'initiative fatigue' among staff. She places significant responsibility on school leaders, arguing that 'leadership impatience' -- the desire to visibly demonstrate momentum through new initiatives and shareable graphics -- is a bigger barrier to real improvement than teacher resistance, and closes with a direct call to reframe professional learning around depth and repetition (returning to the same practice with feedback and coaching) rather than novelty.
points: Wade's central reframe is that professional learning should be iterative, not seasonal -- expertise develops from returning to the same practice repeatedly with feedback, not from sampling new frameworks and moving on.

She names 'leadership impatience' rather than teacher resistance as the bigger barrier to school improvement, arguing leaders chase visible novelty (new frameworks, shareable graphics) that signals progress without actually producing it.

Her implementation-science point is specific and consequential: moving from initial adoption to fidelity 'can take years,' yet schools commonly abandon initiatives after a single term, producing what she calls 'initiative fatigue' among staff.

Wade grounds the argument in personal credibility -- six years of repeatedly presenting on and researching checking for understanding, including attending a colleague's session on the same topic and still leaving with new ideas -- to show expertise doesn't exempt anyone from further refinement.

Her closing formula reframes the goal of PD directly: 'It's not about doing more. It's about doing better' -- shifting the metric of successful professional learning from exposure to depth of implementation.
quotes: Essentially, it’s this myth that if teachers already do something well enough, there’s no point doing any further professional learning on this topic. But what if we’re missing the point of professional learning as a whole?
Expertise does not exempt us from learning. If anything, it increases our responsibility to keep refining.

The problem is, even for topics that do yield greater progress for students or are effective in achieving their aims, expertise doesn’t sufficiently development from tasting. Instead, it develops from returning to the same practice time and time again, applying it consistently and seeking feedback.

Implementation needs to be staged, and moving from initial exploration to implementation with fidelity on a particular technique can take years. Despite this, it isn't uncommon for schools to abandon an initiative after a term.

This drives a cycle of what is really novelty addiction and a prioritisation of visibility over depth. In doing so, leaders, albeit unintentionally, undermine the expertise of their teachers and the entire professional learning process.

Schools that make real impact aren’t about chasing novelty. They double down on what works and refuse to move until it has teeth. Their staff review the same principles time and time again with a focus on doing them better.

As someone working directly in the professional learning space, my biggest learning here is that professional learning isn’t so much about ticking off exposure to new ideas as it is about insisting on improvement. It’s not about doing more. It’s about doing better.
